documentNotes.title: Practical round. Problems to solve
documentNotes.statement: International Remote Astronomy Olympiad. Milan, Italy, 5–13 XI 2021. Task 12: groups α, γ (β crossed out); task 13: α, β, γ; task 14: β, γ. The question pages carry the round label M&I. The text and matching solution/criteria identify the practical round.

documentNotes.title: Printed source details
documentNotes.statement: The introduction calls the objects in task 13 open clusters, while question 13.1 says “globular cluster”; both wordings are retained. Table 14.a prints “rm” for Europa and has handwritten “km” for Ganymede and Callisto. The official solution retains “Sun-Eart”, the table-13.b heading refers to questions 12.1–12.3, and the final diagram prints “12th Nov, 021”. These are source defects, not transcription corrections.

documentNotes.title: Practical Round - Sketches for solutions. For jury job ONLY
documentNotes.statement: These solutions are written for jury members, so they contain some explanations in the form of text. Students are instructed to use only formulas, calculations, drawings, graphs and filling tables. Writing texts is not allowed in the solutions.

documentNotes.title: Reference inventory

It was inspected as reference context; it supplies no additional practical task or requested answer form. The protractor sheet contains three identical copies; one complete copy is reproduced with task 12.

problems.title: Mars motion as seen from the Earth
problems.statement:
Assuming that the orbits of Earth and Mars are circular, picture 12.a shows such orbits to scale; positions of the Sun and of the Earth and Mars when Mars is at opposition are also represented.

In table 12.b you will report distance from Earth and angular data for Mars:

- Column 1: day of observation (in the interval ±105 days from time of opposition $t_0$).
- Column 2: distance to Mars from Earth, to be given in km.
- Column 3: position angle $\alpha$ of Mars, to be given in degrees.
- Column 4: day/days in which Mars is in quadrature with the Sun as seen from Earth (to be indicated by the symbol Q) or it appears “stationing” (to be indicated by the symbol S).

parts.statement: Taking into account the sidereal periods of the Earth and Mars with a good approximation and starting from the initial configuration where Mars is in opposition (i.e. along the up-down direction the orbit representation), compute the positions of the two planets every 15 days for a time interval of ±105 days and draw them on picture 12.a.

sections.statement: In picture 12.a draw the lines connecting the positions of Earth and Mars at the same epoch and, for each epoch, measure:

parts.statement: the Earth-Mars distance $D$ and report it, in km, in column 2 of table 12.b,

the position angle $\alpha$ of Mars as seen from the Earth with reference to the up-down direction (i.e. line connection Earth and Mars when the Mars is at opposition) and report it, in degrees, in column 3 of table 12.b.

Infer in which of the positions of Earth and Mars at the same epoch you have drawn Mars would be in quadrature with the Sun and mark them (one, two or more) with the symbol Q in column 4 of table 12.b.

sections.statement: In picture 12.c report the distance (in au, Y axis) Mars-Earth $D$ as a function of the position angle $\alpha$ (in degrees, X axis).

parts.statement: Infer the days (one, two or more with the precision allowed by the data) when Mars appears stationing in the sky during the considered time interval (±105 days) and mark them with the symbol S in column 4 of table 12.b.
Provide an estimation of the duration of the apparent retrograde motion of Mars $T(\mathrm{retrograde})$ and write it, in days, in the box at the bottom of picture 12.c.

problems.title: Observations at the INAF – Abruzzo Astronomical Observatory (OAAB)
problems.statement:
The observation nights of December 23, 2021, January 24, 2022 and November 25, 2022 are made available at the “TNT” telescope (on photo 13.1.) of the OAAb (geographical coordinates: $\lambda=13^\circ44^\prime$, $\varphi=42^\circ39^\prime$).

The TNT has a Ritchey-Chretien optical design (two mirrors with hyperbolic curvature), with a primary diameter of 720 mm and a secondary of 185 mm. The overall focal length is 9800 mm.

At the focal plane is mounted a back-illuminated E2V CCD47 with $2048\times2048$ square pixels of $20\times20$ micron size each.

You are the scientific manager of a project that aims to study the optical bands of open stellar clusters of our galaxy listed in Table 13.a. In such table you find:

- Column 1: cluster name.
- Columns 2 & 3: right ascension and declination of the cluster.
- Column 4: angular diameter of the cluster.
- Column 5: distance of the cluster in parsecs.

Write in Table 13.b the answers to the following questions:

parts.statement: Choose for each of the three available dates listed in column 1 the globular cluster that at 00:00 Local Time is the nearest at culmination and write its name in column 2.

For each of the three selected clusters infer if it can fit entirely into the field of view of the CCD (i.e. if you can get an image of it with one single acquisition) and write the answer as YES or NO in column 3.
Calculate the radius in light years of the three selected clusters and write them in the column 4.

| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 23 December 2021 |  |  |  |

On Dec 23 the mean Sun has a RA of about $18^{\mathrm h}$. Hence at local midnight the stars closest to culmination have $\mathrm{RA}\simeq6^{\mathrm h}$.

Each day the RA of the mean Sun increase of about $3.93^{\mathrm m}$; from Dec 23 to Jan 24 lasted 32 days, while from 25 Nov to Dec 23 lasted 28 days.

The RA of the mean Sun on 24 Jan is of about $18^{\mathrm h}+32\cdot3.93\simeq20^{\mathrm h}6^{\mathrm m}$ hence at local midnight the stars closest to culmination have $\mathrm{RA}\simeq8^{\mathrm h}6^{\mathrm m}$.

The RA of the mean Sun on 25 Nov is of about $18^{\mathrm h}-28\cdot3.93\simeq16^{\mathrm h}10^{\mathrm m}$ hence at local midnight the stars closest to culmination have $\mathrm{RA}\simeq4^{\mathrm h}10^{\mathrm m}$.

The length of each CCD side is $2048\cdot20\cdot10^{-6}\,\mathrm m\simeq41\,\mathrm{mm}$. Taking into account the focal length of the telescope the FoV is a square with a side of $\alpha=\arctan\frac{41\,\mathrm{mm}}{9800\,\mathrm{mm}}\simeq14^\prime$

Given the angular diameter $\beta$ and the distance $D$ of the clusters, the radius $R$, after transforming the distance in ly can be computed using the formula:

$$R=D\cdot\tan\frac{\beta}{2}$$

problems.title: Galilean Moons
problems.statement:
Let’s assume Jupiter equator and the orbits of its four Galilean Moons be coincident with the ecliptic. The position of Galilean Moons on 1st of November 2021, as observed from Earth, is shown in Figure 14.1. The in-scale corresponding orbital configuration, as could be observed from a distant point located on the extension Jupiter rotation axis, is shown in Figure 14.2, where the direction to Earth is represented as a dot-and-dash line.

The basic data for the four Galilean Moons of Jupiter are given in Table 14.a:

- Column 1: Moon name.
- Column 2: Semi-major axis in km.
- Column 3: Sidereal period (day, hours, minutes).
- Column 4: Azimuth on 1st November 2021 in degrees as measured anticlockwise with respect to Earth direction.

All moons orbits have a very low eccentricity and then they can be considered circular. The Jupiter average radius is assumed to be 69173 km.

parts.statement:
Draw in Figure 14.3 what will be the observed orbital configurations for observations made at the same hour in the following dates:

3rd of November, 2021

4th of November, 2021

5th of November, 2021

8th of November, 2021

9th of November, 2021

10th of November, 2021

12th of November, 2021.

Taking into account the poor spatial resolution of Galileo’s telescope, one of the computed 2021 configurations appears quite similar (although not identical) to one of the 1610 configurations observed by Galileo that are shown in Figure 14.4.
Which one of the 2021 configurations is similar to one of the 1610 configurations? Write in English the two dates in the box below Figure 14.4.
